Quantitative Research Note

Why Cheap-Looking Charts Keep Falling: Notes on Moving-Average Discipline

Observations from 26.8 years of public US equity price and volume series (2000–2026).

AV
Arthur Vance
Senior Portfolio Research Note · 2026-11-20 · 6 min read

One of the hardest habits to unlearn in equity investing is anchoring to last year's peak price. When a well-known stock drops thirty-five or forty percent from its high, it looks like a bargain on a one-year chart even if revenue estimates are still falling and institutions are quietly reducing exposure.

Across our 26.8-year historical archive of liquid US equities (2000–2026), stocks trading beneath declining twenty-day and sixty-day moving averages exhibited noticeably wider downside variance than cohorts that had first stabilized above their medium-term averages on expanding volume.

Rather than guessing bottoms in falling single-stock trends, most retirement households anchor core wealth in broad non-leveraged sector pillars ($SMH and $XLV) plus short-term US Treasury reserves ($SGOV). For readers who also study individual companies such as $MSFT or $CELH, our public factor archive records four plain measurements: distance from the trailing 52-week high, stabilization distance above the 52-week low, daily close relative to the 20-day and 60-day moving averages, and 10-day relative volume.

None of those four numbers predicts the future, and past cohort behavior never guarantees tomorrow's return. What they offer is a calm, repeatable checklist—a way to verify whether a price trend has actually stabilized before committing hard-earned capital.
